courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.contribution: Arguments/fallacies, debate/speech delivery and actual educational climate/community storytelling supply specific public-communication tools for accountable policy and social participation. It is complementary to political analysis, not a political-science substitute.

evidenceFields.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
evidenceFields.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidenceFields.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidenceFields.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

courses.name: Dutch
courses.contribution: Beginner Dutch, functional communication and cultural comparison provide a bounded local-language/cultural-access complement to community inquiry. Groningen’s Language&Culture is linguistics/anthropology, so language proficiency alone does not replace it.

evidenceFields.description2: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops beginner Dutch for everyday oral and written communication while introducing Dutch culture. Speaking and listening receive particular emphasis, supported by pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, reading and functional writing. Students practise introductions, family conversations, shopping, travel and leisure through dialogues, role-play and short written tasks. Cultural work includes research and presentations in English, engagement with Dutch film and music, and comparison with students’ own cultural contexts.
evidenceFields.topics: Dutch pronunciation and spelling; Everyday vocabulary for introductions, family, shopping, travel and leisure; Verb conjugation and the perfect tense; Pronouns and possession; Negation; Main- and subordinate-clause word order; Adjectives, comparatives and superlatives; Functional reading and writing; Everyday Dutch cultural practices; Cross-cultural comparison
evidenceFields.methods: Dutch pronunciation practice; Dialogue construction and conversational role-play; Functional writing in Dutch; Comparative cultural analysis

courses.name: Persuasive Communication
courses.contribution: Coactive persuasion/framing/cognitive shortcuts and actual sustainability communication implementation support public argument and local action. The documented projects concern circular lifestyles, not a guaranteed government/health campaign.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
evidenceFields.discipline: Communication studies; Social psychology; Applied ethics
evidenceFields.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
evidenceFields.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.contribution: Actual racial construction/power, marginalized/Indigenous media, participant observation, archives, documentary podcast and PhotoVoice give a substantive culture/race/reflexive interpretation contribution to inclusion. The American cultural-history focus is narrower than Groningen’s linguistics/anthropology diversity.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
evidenceFields.discipline: Cultural history; Media studies; Race and ethnicity studies; American studies
evidenceFields.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
evidenceFields.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

schedules.label: Energy, climate & environmental resources
schedules.concept: Studies climate and energy transitions through environmental science, biodiversity, water and material resources. Combines field and data methods with economics and sustainability governance.

schedules.label: Politics, law & political economy
schedules.concept: A governance-centred route addressing global inequality, institutions, international law, ethical responsibility, conflict and political economy through political science, philosophy, law, economics and social research.

schedules.label: Culture, social inclusion & health
schedules.concept: Study social inclusion and well-being through cultural, rights-based and psychological perspectives. Combine epidemiology and health psychology with historical injustice, media representation, community research, institutions and environmental justice; this does not reproduce a full global-health sequence.

scheduleFinding: All three unchanged course sets and term assignments pass current workbook feasibility in a reduced temporary UCR-only input. This is mechanical confirmation of internal prototypes, not a full external schema or approved comparison.
contributionCorrection: Replaced all53repeated generic contribution statements with actual code-specific subject/method functions and direct/complementary limits. Existing course choices and exact schedules survive independent reassessment; no arbitrary substitutions or offering/database changes.
conceptAssessment: The environmental prototype has actual climate/energy, Earth/soil/water, resource and data/governance functions; ecology is represented through biodiversity/nature-based processes rather than a deep ecosystem sequence. The political prototype combines real institutions, rights/international law, political economy, normative thought and historical power with public argument. The third studies culture/inclusion and well-being with explicit psychological/epidemiological contributions; its substantial institutional/history/rights weight is not relabelled a full global-health degree. Accurate internal labels replace broad formal-major lookalikes. All remain provisional: full GRL comparability, strongest closest response, sequential inclusion/stopping and final alignments depend on the unresolved65EC.

y1-human: Social cognition, influence and discrimination overlap with the social component. Groningen also introduces individual, cultural and environmental explanations.
y1-it: Both develop computational data handling. Groningen additionally teaches digital literacy and responsible AI. Its Python/QGIS and AI/security content is not reproduced simply by UCR’s R data-handling tools.
y1-earth: Earth-system environmental change and human pressures overlap. Dynamic Earth and Climate Change add geoscience and climate, respectively.
y1-language: Shared critical interpretation of race, representation and cultural power, with reflexive/cross-cultural inquiry, supplies a substantive partial relationship. WUR adds linguistics/anthropology and wider cultural diversity; beginner Dutch alone is not its equivalent.
y1-health: Both address population health and its determinants. The UCR course focuses on epidemiological measures and study design. WUR also studies historical/structural and global-health governance and runs community campaigns; UCR’s needs-assessment project does not guarantee the same campaign.
y1-politics: International actors, power and organisations overlap. Groningen uses the SDGs as a framework.
y1-energy: Both consider sustainable energy and its transition. UCR includes energy yield and renewable technologies.
y1-econ: Both introduce markets, choice, production and macroeconomic questions.
y1-qual: Both develop qualitative project design, data collection and interpretation.
y1-stats-1: Both develop descriptive statistics and basic inference. UCR combines these with wider research design.
y2-leadership: Both develop reflection and personal learning. PPD also teaches academic practices.
y2-stats-2: Shared regression/inference, causal versus predictive reasoning, model assessment and simulation provide a specific applied-method relationship. WUR covers broader climate/energy/public-health uncertainty and risk; UCR uses economic models and Stata.
y2-ethics: Both compare normative reasoning. Groningen focuses specifically on global responsibilities.
y2-living-lab: The UCR sustainability project supports stakeholder research. Groningen requires a dedicated research internship and partner-facing outputs.
y3-minor: Open minor space has no single course counterpart.
y3-capstone: The capstone combines thesis and portfolio. A course research paper or optional UCR research does not replace this requirement.

alignmentCorrections: Language&Culture has a substantive cultural-race/reflexive relationship to Media&Race; Dutch proficiency alone is insufficient.
StatisticsII has a specific applied regression/inference relationship to Econometrics; DataScience alone is not a second statistics course.

LivingLab relates to actual external-stakeholder sustainability research with different topic/credit/entry structure; UCR course is available only in2026h2, so its early placement is retained under its actual NONE prerequisite, without claiming GRL progression equivalence.
Capstone and minor remain unmatched; a course paper does not certify required thesis/portfolio or unspecified open-space content.
